Here is the itemized extraction of J. B. Lightfoot's explicit positions and claims across the substantive and extended B001 items in his commentary, Saint Paul's Epistle to the Galatians: A Revised Text with Introduction, Notes, and Dissertations (1914 edition / 1890 10th edition text).
B001-12: Galatians 3:13 / Deuteronomy 21:23
S04F-E001
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E001
B001 Passage ID: B001-12
Author's Claim: The Hebrew construct phrase קללת אלהים in Deuteronomy 21:23 contains a grammatical ambiguity, allowing אלהים to be rendered either as a subjective genitive ("accursed of God") or an objective genitive ("an insult/reproach to God").
Supporting Quotation: "The ambiguity arises out of the construction of אלהים, since the case attached to קללת may denote either the person who pronounces the curse... or the person against whom the curse is pronounced"
1
.
Printed Page Number: Page 152
NotebookLM Citation:
1
Textual Evidence Invoked: Hebrew construct phrase קללת אלהים in Deut 21:23 compared with Judges 9:57 (subjective genitive) and Genesis 27:13 (objective genitive)
1
.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Textual-critical
Qualifications / Conditions: Depending on whether a subjective or objective genitive is assigned, two distinct interpretations emerge
1
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E002
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E002
B001 Passage ID: B001-12
Author's Claim: Paul adopts the rendering of the Septuagint (κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ) in substance, but instinctively omits ὑπὸ Θεοῦ in Galatians 3:13 because Christ was in no literal sense accursed by God.
Supporting Quotation: "He was in no literal sense κατάρατος ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, and St Paul instinctively omits those words which do not strictly apply"
2
.
Printed Page Number: Page 140 (also p. 152)
1
2
NotebookLM Citation:
1
2
Textual Evidence Invoked: LXX rendering κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ vs. Paul's shortened citation in Galatians 3:13 (ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου)
1
2
.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Textual-critical
Qualifications / Conditions: If ὑπὸ Θεοῦ had been added, it would have required theological qualification
2
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E003
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E003
B001 Passage ID: B001-12
Author's Claim: The rendering "he that hangeth is a reproach/insult to God" became the popular Jewish and Ebionite interpretation from the second century onward to ward off the reproach of a crucified Messiah and turn the text against Roman persecutors or Christian opponents.
Supporting Quotation: "This seems to have been the popular Jewish interpretation... shared therefore by Jewish Christians... at all events from the second century of the Christian era."
1
.
Printed Page Number: Pages 152–153
1
3
NotebookLM Citation:
1
3
Textual Evidence Invoked: Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion; Siphri on Deuteronomy; Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan; Ebionite Gospel; Ariston of Pella (Dispute of Jason and Papiscus); Justin Martyr (Dial. c. Tryph. c. 96); Tertullian (Adv. Judaeos § 10)
1
3
.
Claim Type: Historical / Exegetical
Qualifications / Conditions: Jewish patriots impaled or crucified by foreign rulers made it intolerable that God's curse should attach to them, prompting a rendering that turned the reproach against the persecutors
3
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E004
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E004
B001 Passage ID: B001-12
Author's Claim: Although Deuteronomy 21:23 originally referred to the impalement or gibbeting of a malefactor's body after execution rather than death by crucifixion, Paul's application of the passage to Christ's crucifixion is entirely legitimate because the law attached ignominy to the hanging itself.
Supporting Quotation: "For though this passage did not contemplate death by crucifixion, the application was quite legitimate. It was the hanging, not the death, that brought ignominy"
4
.
Printed Page Number: Page 154
4
NotebookLM Citation:
4
Textual Evidence Invoked: Hebrew verb תלה (hanged); Chaldee paraphrase of Deuteronomy; Peshito Syriac usage in Galatians 3:1; Jewish derogatory term תלוי ("the gibbeted one")
4
.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Methodological
Qualifications / Conditions: Ancient Jews considered hanging after death and crucifixion as essentially the same punishment in terms of ignominy and defilement of the land
4
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
B001-1: Genesis 15:6 / Galatians 3:6 / Romans 4:3
S04F-E005
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E005
B001 Passage ID: B001-1
Author's Claim: In Genesis 15:6, the Hebrew text reads וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה ("and [He] imputed it to him [for] righteousness"), which Paul quotes verbatim from the Septuagint in Galatians 3:6 and Romans 4:3.
Supporting Quotation: "It is quoted as in the LXX also in Rom. iv. 3, James ii. 23, Clem. Rom. § 10, Justin Dial. c. Tryph. § 119."
5
.
Printed Page Number: Page 136
5
NotebookLM Citation:
5
Textual Evidence Invoked: Hebrew MT וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה vs. LXX rendering ἐπίστευσεν Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην cited in Gal 3:6, Rom 4:3, Jas 2:23, 1 Clem 10, and Justin Dial. 119
5
.
Claim Type: Textual-critical / Exegetical
Qualifications / Conditions: Barnabas § 13 quotes the passage too loosely with an obvious infusion of Paul's language to infer its underlying text
5
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E006
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E006
B001 Passage ID: B001-1
Author's Claim: By the time of the Christian era, Genesis 15:6 had become a standard theological thesis discussed in both Alexandrian (Philonic) and Rabbinic schools, preparing the way for the Apostolic teaching on faith.
Supporting Quotation: "there is, I think, sufficient evidence to show that at the time of the Christian era the passage in Genesis relating to Abraham's faith had become a standard text in the Jewish schools"
6
.
Printed Page Number: Page 159
6
NotebookLM Citation:
6
Textual Evidence Invoked: 1 Maccabees 2:52; Philo (De Migr. Abr., De Abrah., Quis Rer. Div. Her., De Mutat. Nom.); 4 Ezra; Mechilta on Exodus 14:31; Siphri on Deuteronomy 11:13
6
.
Claim Type: Historical / Methodological
Qualifications / Conditions: The importance of the text was felt in both Alexandrian and Rabbinic schools, though the lessons deduced from it differed widely
6
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E007
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E007
B001 Passage ID: B001-1
Author's Claim: Philo comments on Genesis 15:6 at least ten times, viewing Abraham's faith as the "queen of virtues," but allegorizes his life as the individual soul's progress toward God rather than a historical or covenantal community.
Supporting Quotation: "To him it was not a history, but an allegory; or, if a history as well, it was as such of infinitely little importance."
7
.
Printed Page Number: Pages 159–160
6
7
NotebookLM Citation:
6
7
Textual Evidence Invoked: Philo's treatises (Leg. Alleg., Quod Deus Imm., De Migr. Abr., Quis Rer. Div. Her., De Mutat. Nom., De Abrah., De Praem. et Poen., De Nob.)
6
7
.
Claim Type: Historical / Literary
Qualifications / Conditions: Philo appreciated the personal significance of Abraham's faith, but the idea of a chosen people or Church was absent from his thought
8
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E008
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E008
B001 Passage ID: B001-1
Author's Claim: Rabbinic tradition (as in the Mechilta on Exod 14:31) treated Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6 as a meritorious work ("the merit of faith") that earned righteousness and the inheritance of both worlds for his descendants.
Supporting Quotation: "In like manner thou findest that Abraham our father inherited this world and the world to come solely by the merit of faith whereby he believed in the Lord"
9
.
Printed Page Number: Page 162
9
NotebookLM Citation:
9
Textual Evidence Invoked: Mechilta on Exod 14:31; Siphri on Deut 11:13; later Rabbinic commentary on Genesis 15:6 (interpreting the second clause as "Abraham counted on God's righteousness")
9
.
Claim Type: Historical / Exegetical
Qualifications / Conditions: Later Rabbinic writers altered the interpretation of the second clause to "Abraham counted on God's righteousness" specifically to counter Paul's inference of justification by faith
9
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S04F-E009
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E009
B001 Passage ID: B001-1
Author's Claim: The apparent contradiction between Paul (Rom 3:28 / Gal 3:6) and James (Jas 2:24) regarding Genesis 15:6 vanishes when recognized as independent responses to diverse Jewish school interpretations—Paul opposing Pharisaic reliance on outward works, James opposing a barren orthodoxy.
Supporting Quotation: "the facts collected above destroy the force of any argument founded on the mere coincidence of the examples chosen."
10
.
Printed Page Number: Page 164
10
NotebookLM Citation:
10
Textual Evidence Invoked: Genesis 15:6 quoted in Rom 3:28, Gal 3:6, Jas 2:24; Michaelis; Neander (Pflanzung p. 567); Justin (Dial. p. 370D); Clementine Homilies (iii. 6)
10
.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Historical
Qualifications / Conditions: Whether James directly targeted Pharisaic barren orthodoxy or misplaced reliance on Paul's teaching must be determined by detailed examination of James, but their circles of labor were unlikely to intersect
10
.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
B001-8: 1 Corinthians 1:19 / Isaiah 29:14 (Cross-Reference)
S04F-E010
Proposed Evidence ID: S04F-E010
B001 Passage ID: B001-8
Author's Claim: In Galatians 2:21, the verb ἀθετῶ means "to nullify" or "to set at nought," sharing the exact sense used in 1 Corinthians 1:19 and Luke 7:30.
Supporting Quotation: "For ἀθετῶ 'to nullify' see Luke vii. 30, 1 Cor. i. 19: its exact sense here is fixed by δωρεὰν ἀπέθανεν."
11

Printed Page Number: Page 120
11

11
Textual Evidence Invoked: Usage of ἀθετέω in Galatians 2:21, 1 Corinthians 1:19, Luke 7:30, and LXX Psalm 33:7

Claim Type: Exegetical / Literary
Qualifications / Conditions: None

The passage in Deuteronomy, it is true, does not refer directly to cruci- fixion as a means of execution, but to impaling bodies after death. It has been said indeed that Philo’ speaks of the impalement there mentioned as a mode of putting to death, but this seems to be a mistake. Philo says, that Moses would have put such malefactors to death ten thousand times over if it were possible, but not being able to kill them more than once, he adds another penalty, ordering murderers to be gibbeted (ripwpiav ddAnv mpoodiatatrerat KeXev@v Tos aveAovtas avacKkvdomi¢er Oa). Nor, so far as I  am aware, is there any evidence to show that the Jews at the time of the Christian era interpreted the passage of death by crucifixion. Crucifixion was not a Jewish punishment. The evangelist (Joh. xviil. 32) sees a pro- vidence in the delivering over of our Lord to the Romans to be put to death, so that He might die in the manuer He himself had foretold. It had been employed occasionally in seasons of tumult by their own princes’, but was regarded as an act of great atrocity. Even the Roman looked upon crucifixion with abhorrence*. To the Jew it was especially hateful,  owing in part no doubt to the curse attaching to this ignominious exposure of the body in the passage of Deuteronomy. For though this passage did not contemplate death by crucifixion, the application was quite legitimate. It was the hanging, not the death, that brought ignominy on the sufferer and defilement on the land. Hence the Chaldee paraphrase of Deutero- nomy employs the same word (aby) which is used in several places in the Peshito Syriac to describe the crucifixion of our Lord (e.g. Gal. iii. 1). Hence also later Jews, speaking of Jesus, called Him by the same name of reproach (\5n, ‘the gibbeted one’), which they found in the original text of the lawgiver*. It was not that they mistook the meaning of the word, but that they considered the two punishments essentially the same. No Jew would have questioned the propriety of St Paul's application of the text to our Lord. The curse pronounced in the law was interpreted and strengthened by the national sentiment. EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS,  If we look only to the individual man, faith with Philo is substantially the same as faith with St Paul. The lessons drawn from the history of Abraham by the Alexandrian Jew and the Christian Apostle differ very slightly. Faith is the postponement of all present aims and desires, the sacrifice of all material interests, to the Infinite and Unseen. But the  philosopher of Alexandria saw no historical bearing in the career of Abraham. As he was severed from the heart of the nation, so the pulses  of the national life had ceased to beat in him. The idea of a chosen people retained scarcely the faintest hold on his thoughts. Hence the only lesson which he drew from the patriarch’s life had reference to himself. Abraham was but a type, a symbol of the individual man. The promises made to him, the rich inheritance, the numerous progeny, had no fulfilment except  in the growth of his own character. The Alexandrian Jew, like the heathen philosopher, was exclusive, isolated, selfish. With him the theo- cracy of the Old Testament was emptied of all its meaning: the covenant was a matter between God and his own spirit. The idea of a Church did not enter into his reckoning. He appreciated the significance of Abraham’s  Jaith, but Abraham’s seed was almost meaningless to him. On the other hand Judaism proper was strong where Alexandrian  Judaism was weak, and weak where it was strong. The oppressive rule of  Syrians and Romans had served only to develope and strengthen the national feeling. ‘We are Abraham’s sous, we have Abraham to our father’: such was their religious war-cry, full of meaning to every true Israelite. It was a protest against selfish isolation. It spoke of a corporate life, of national hopes and interests, of an outward community, a common brotherhood, ruled by the same laws and animated by the same feelings. In other words, it kept alive the idea of a Church. This was the point of contact between St Paul’s teaching and Rabbinical Judaism. But their agreement does not go much beyond this. With them indeed he upheld the faith of Abraham as an example to Abraham’s descendants. But, while they interpreted it as a rigorous observance of outward ordi- nances, he understood by it a spiritual state, a steadfast reliance on the unseen God. With them too he clung to the fulfilment of the promise, he cherished fondly the privileges of a son of Abraham. But to him the link of brotherhood was no longer the same blood, but the same spirit: they only were Abraham’s sons who inherited Abraham’s faith.  Thus the coincidences and contrasts of St Paul’s doctrine of faith and of his application of Abraham’s history with the teaching of the Jewish doctors  are equally instructive. With the Alexandrian school it looked to the growth of the individual man, with the Rabbinical it recognised the claims of the society : with the one it was spiritual, with the other it was historical. On the other hand, it was a protest alike against the selfish, esoteric, individual- ising spirit of the one, and the narrow, slavish formalism of the other.  This sketch is very far from doing justice to St Paul’s doctrine of faith. In order fully to understand its force, or indeed to appreciate its leading conception, it would be necessary to take into account the atoning death and resurrection of Christ as the central object on which that faith is fixed.
